cases.provenance: A human reviewer flagged this defect in an inline comment on the reviewed pull request.
cases.description:
See https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/issues/15029#issuecomment-800690344 you can't just link the `libssl` and `libcrypto` symlinks to the OpenSSL 1.1.x version and just expect it to work. It does allow the library to load but causes a hard fault in the process as soon as `libmi` tries to access any of the OpenSSL libraries in that. OpenSSL 1.1.x and 1.0.x (what `libmi` that is shipped by PowerShell is linked to) are not API and ABI compatible.

You need to either link it to OpenSSL 1.0.x and document the `compat-openssl10` (other whatever package provides OpenSSL 1.0.x on the distro) requirement for WSMan work or ship a recompiled `libmi` against OpenSSL 1.1.x so it can use a modern OpenSSL version.

evidence.thread_resolution:
iSazonov: > ship a recompiled libmi against OpenSSL 1.1.x

If I remember correctly this is blocked by external team.

------------------

We could try to load libmi and the old openssl to alternative ALC. I hope AssemblyLoadContext.LoadUnmanagedDll() will do this. If yes it is not too huge work. /cc @rjmholt
jborean93: There’s a long history behind it, PowerShell can always just recompile the libraries from the same source and ship it. It’s not like the team maintains it anyway so I never understood the support argument. Even now the version shipped by PowerShell is missing a lot of security features and contains bugs so what use is the support argument if it’s not being acted upon anyway. But this has been commented on quite a lot of times and ultimately the team isn’t interested in doing this. All this doesn’t mean the package should point the link to the wrong OpenSSL version.

> I hope AssemblyLoadContext.LoadUnmanagedDll() will do this

I don’t think so, the linking happened at the unmanaged layer. PowerShell isn’t loading libcrypto, libssl, or even libmi directly. It’s loading libpsrpclient and whatever the native loading mechanism is loading libmi/libssl.

Ultimately you just can’t try and use libssl from 1.1.x when the calling code is expecting the symbols and API from the 1.0.x version. It might be enough to get libmi to load but as soon as you try and open a https connection it will crash the entire process. If the goal is to try and lessen the dependency on OpenSSL 1.0.x for WSMan then this is the wrong thing to do. It’s still a dependency and now you are introducing process crashes when it tried to access libssl.
iSazonov: > I don’t think so, the linking happened at the unmanaged layer. PowerShell isn’t loading libcrypto, libssl, or even libmi directly. It’s loading libpsrpclient and whatever the native loading mechanism is loading libmi/libssl.

In that case, it doesn't matter at all - it didn't work before and won't work now - nothing has changed.
jborean93: It does still matter, if we look at the PowerShell codebase we can see the various PInvoke definitions for the WSMan api are being called through [libpsrpclient](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/2784add414393b0ecab798055cfbac0d363c1c1e/src/System.Management.Automation/engine/remoting/fanin/WSManNativeAPI.cs#L2339). On non-Windows this is essentially a build of https://github.com/PowerShell/psl-omi-provider and is designed to replicate the Windows WSMan layer and is dynamically linked to `libmi` which is where the actual WSMan client is implemented.

The crux of this problem is what `libmi` is dyamically linked to. In both the version provided for EL7 and EL8 we can see that they are both linked against OpenSSL 1.0.x.
